clue.text: Marine message received — looks black !

parts.note: a Royal Marine is nicknamed a 'jolly' in old naval slang
radio operators say 'roger' to confirm a message has been received

explanation.surface: A sailor gets a signal and frowns darkly at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks black' is a playful definition: the pirate flag is the thing that looks black. A Royal Marine was called a 'jolly' in old navy slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The pirate flag is a black banner bearing a skull, so it is the emblem that looks black.

clue.text: Sound stuff to catch a monkey!

indicators.note: the word is said aloud and the spoken form gives the letters entered

parts.note: Jacko is an old pet name for a monkey, and a net is what catches it

explanation.surface: Advice on the right material for trapping an escaped monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' means cloth here, not things. Said aloud, 'Jacko net' (a net for a monkey, Jacko being a traditional monkey name) sounds like the name of the cotton fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a light cotton fabric, and 'stuff' is an old word for woven cloth.

clue.text: Quadriennial springs ?

parts.note: read 'springs' as jumps rather than the season: years named for a leap that come round every four years

explanation.surface: A spring season that comes only once every four years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Springs' looks like the season, but it means leaps: the years with an extra day, coming every fourth year, are named after a jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Years with a 29 February occur every four years and are named for a jump, a spring.

clue.text: Marks of servitude are all right in agreement

indicators.note: the letters for 'all right' are placed inside the word for agreement

parts.note: saying yes is giving agreement
OK means all right

explanation.surface: Signs of slavery are acceptable when everyone consents.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden frame laid on a subject's neck was the classic token of subjugation, so these are marks of servitude.

clue.text: As Kipps announced he was, both sides

definitions.text: As Kipps announced he was, both sides

parts.words: As Kipps announced he was, both sides
parts.note: Kipps, the H. G. Wells hero, told people he had lost his parents on both sides, father and mother

explanation.surface: A character declaring his family status on both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipps is the hero of H. G. Wells's novel, raised by an aunt and uncle because both his parents were dead, which he announces in his h-dropping speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing father and mother, both sides of the family, leaves a child parentless.

clue.text: Where Lancashire takes the cake !

parts.note: a Lancashire town gives its name to a famous currant pastry, so the county wins a prize there

explanation.surface: Lancashire comes top somewhere, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the cake' sounds like the idiom for being outstanding, but read literally it is the town in Lancashire that gives its name to a flaky currant pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: The town near Manchester, historically in Lancashire, gave its name to a round currant-filled pastry.

clue.text: Bird that classically turns to itself

indicators.note: the Latin word for 'to itself' turns round, read from right to left

parts.note: the Latin dative 'sibi' means 'to itself'; 'classically' says the word is Latin

explanation.surface: A bird of classical times that keeps turning back on itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classically' says the word for 'to itself' is Latin: SIBI. 'Turns' reverses it to give the wading bird sacred to the ancient Egyptians.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a long-billed wading bird, sacred in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Middleman in a tub

parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Rub-a-dub-dub, three men in a tub' lists three tradesmen; this is the one named second

explanation.surface: A broker who conducts his business from a bathtub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middleman' looks like a broker, but it is the middle one of the three men in the tub in the nursery rhyme: the butcher, this tradesman and the candlestick-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the three men are butcher, bread-maker and candlestick-maker, and the bread-maker stands in the middle.

clue.text: " And all for love, and nothing for reward" he wrote

definitions.text: " And all for love, and nothing for reward" he wrote

parts.words: And all for love, and nothing for reward" he wrote
parts.note: the line ends a sonnet in the Elizabethan poet's sequence Amoretti; the solver names its author

explanation.surface: A selfless sentiment, quoted with its author left for the reader to name.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a general-knowledge clue: the quoted line is from the Amoretti sonnets of the Elizabethan poet who also wrote The Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund, the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene, wrote this line in his Amoretti sonnets.

clue.text: A draw at close of play ?

definitions.text: A draw at close of play ?

parts.words: A draw at close of play
parts.note: read 'draw' as the pulling across of stage drapes when a performance ends, not a tied match

explanation.surface: A match that ends level when stumps are pulled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A draw at close of play' sounds like a tied game, but it is the stage drapes drawn across when a theatre play ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage drapes are drawn across at the end of a theatre performance.

clue.text: Go to pieces, perhaps, with praise

definitions.meaning: to break down, mentally or physically, is to go to pieces
to talk something up, to extol it highly, is an informal sense

explanation.surface: Someone collapses emotionally after being complimented.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to break down under strain and, informally, to talk up or extol, as in 'not all it's cracked up to be'.

clue.text: Laughter at a hen-party ?

parts.note: read 'hen-party' as a gathering of real hens, whose clucking noise is 'chuck'

explanation.surface: Giggling at a bride's night out with her friends.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen party is a bride-to-be's night out, but here it is a gathering of actual hens, and 'chuck' is the noise a hen makes, so their laughter is a quiet clucking laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiet laugh, here pictured as the clucking of hens, whose call is 'chuck'.

clue.text: A sound poet ?

parts.note: the surname of an English poet is said like the word for a din, so he is a poet who is a sound

explanation.surface: A praise for a reliable, competent versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' seems to mean reliable, but the poet Alfred, author of The Highwayman, has a surname pronounced like a word for a loud din.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, author of The Highwayman, has a surname pronounced exactly like a word for a racket.

clue.text: They provide openings for super rate reform

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so the letters of the two words are made into a new form

explanation.surface: A political promise of opportunities through an overhaul of the top tax band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' rearranges the letters of SUPER and RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaps or holes are openings, as in a camera's light hole.

clue.text: Designing paper, hot from the press

definitions.text: Designing paper, hot from the press

parts.words: Designing paper, hot from the press
parts.note: read as a sheet carrying a design that is pressed on with a hot iron, not a newspaper fresh off the presses

explanation.surface: A scheming newspaper, freshly printed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Designing paper, hot from the press' suggests a scheming newspaper just printed, but it is decorative paper whose pattern is moved onto cloth with a hot iron or press.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheet bearing a design that is moved onto fabric or china by heat and pressure.

clue.text: Telltale footwear

definitions.meaning: one who sneaks, informs on others, is a telltale
soft-soled canvas shoes, named for their quietness

explanation.surface: Shoes that give away where someone has been.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sneaks to teachers is a tattler, and soft rubber-soled shoes are named for silent movement.

clue.text: Namely, that is right for a Mohammedan

parts.note: viz. is the abbreviation meaning namely

explanation.surface: Someone explaining what is correct for a Muslim believer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mohammedan' is a dated term for a Muslim; the definition is a high official of a Muslim state.
explanation.definitionFit: A high minister in old Muslim states such as the Ottoman empire, so a Muslim official.

clue.text: I throw my weight about in North London

parts.note: to sling is to throw
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone boasting of bullying people across the north of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a bully swaggering round north London, but 'my' and 'about' are only links; 'in North London' is a loose definition of the borough itself.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an inner borough in the north of London.

clue.text: Maritime attendance at early weekend fixtures?

definitions.note: an adjective standing for the seagoing warships themselves

parts.note: Friday, abbreviated Fri, is the early start of the weekend
a gate is the number of spectators at a sporting fixture; several such crowds are gates

explanation.surface: Crowds at sea-themed matches played at the start of the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gates' is the British term for crowd numbers at football matches (fixtures). The definition 'Maritime' is loose: these are seagoing warships.
explanation.definitionFit: These are fast naval warships, vessels of the sea.

clue.text: It's curdled, so step out for a drink

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone told to leave a pub because the milk has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges the letters of SO STEP. 'It's curdled' fits too: the drink is hot milk curdled with ale or wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot drink of milk curdled with ale or wine, often spiced.

clue.text: Taken hot at dinner in Lancs?

definitions.text: Taken hot at dinner in Lancs

parts.words: Taken hot at dinner in Lancs
parts.note: a Lancashire meal is a stewed hotpot, and taking a chance on whatever dish is served is a gamble at dinner

explanation.surface: A diner in Lancashire served a dish straight from the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints 'Lancs', short for Lancashire, home of the hotpot stew. The phrase means taking whatever happens to be on offer for a meal, a chance on what is in the cooking vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a meal of whatever is available, a chance on what is in the cooking vessel.

clue.text: Army watch for instance ?

parts.note: read 'Army' as 'arm-y', belonging to the arm: a timepiece strapped on the arm is an example

explanation.surface: A timepiece issued to soldiers, given as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army' looks like the military, but read as arm-y (to do with the arm) it points to a band worn round the wrist, a watch being one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A band or strap worn round the lower arm, such as a watch strap.

clue.text: Bunglers on the mend

definitions.meaning: travelling menders of pots and pans worked at mending

explanation.surface: Incompetent people somehow recovering.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy fumblers are so called, and so are travelling repairers of pots and pans, always busy mending.

clue.text: Sleeping fish ?

parts.note: a 'kip' is a sleep, so a smoked herring is read as a sleeper

explanation.surface: A fish dozing at the bottom of the tank.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'kip' is British slang for a nap, so the smoked herring is pictured as a fish that is asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoked split herring, whose name also suggests someone who takes a 'kip', a nap.

clue.text: Dropping a fish to conjure with?

parts.note: a conjuror performs a trick
a ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A magician's fish that gets let fall during the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping' means falling in drops, not letting go.
explanation.definitionFit: Water falling in drops or a thin stream is dripping down, dropping drop by drop.

clue.text: Hardly a ghost-writer. Ghosts, yes

parts.note: a ghost-writer works anonymously for others; the Norwegian playwright wrote under his own name a play called Ghosts

explanation.surface: A writer famous in his own right, not a hired hack.
explanation.walkthrough: A ghost-writer writes books published under someone else's name; this famous Norwegian dramatist wrote the play Ghosts (1881) under his own.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik, the Norwegian dramatist, wrote the play Ghosts, so he is a writer of Ghosts but no hired anonymous author.

clue.text: Cleric encourages the food preservers

parts.note: tins, called cans, preserve food
to urge someone on is to encourage them; 'on!' is a cry of encouragement

explanation.surface: A clergyman cheering on the people bottling jam.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as a cheer to tins: 'Can, on!'
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman attached to a cathedral chapter.

clue.text: " Has crossed the nadir, and begins to" (Housman)

definitions.text: " Has crossed the nadir, and begins to" (Housman)

parts.words: Has crossed the nadir, and begins to" (Housman
parts.note: the missing last word of A. E. Housman's line is a verb for going up again after the lowest point

explanation.surface: A quoted line of poetry with its final word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: once past the nadir, its lowest point, the thing can only rise, which gives the missing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: After the lowest point the natural next move is to ascend, the word that completes the line.

clue.text: Run past clumsily to open the case

indicators.note: letters handled clumsily get jumbled, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller runs past a suitcase awkwardly while trying to open it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clumsily' rearranges the letters of RUN PAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Undoing the strap that fastens a case or bag lets it open.

clue.text: The order is a growing one for Scotland

definitions.text: The order is a growing one for Scotland

parts.words: The order is a growing one for Scotland
parts.note: Scotland's highest order of chivalry is named after the country's plant emblem, a living thing that grows

explanation.surface: Something about orders increasing north of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The order' looks like a growing pile of orders, but it is Scotland's chivalric order, named after the prickly plant that is Scotland's national emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: The prickly plant is Scotland's emblem and gives its name to the Order of chivalry for Scots.

clue.text: Pharaoh found them dreamy !

parts.note: in Genesis, Pharaoh dreams of seven fat and seven lean cows, the old word for cattle being wanted

explanation.surface: An Egyptian king swooning over someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreamy' suggests attraction, but in Genesis, Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat and seven lean cattle, interpreted by Joseph; the answer is the archaic plural for cows.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic plural for cows, as in the Bible's account of Pharaoh's dream of fat and lean cattle.

clue.text: Transverse emblem of 1 ac.

parts.note: the pirate flag at 1 across shows a skull above two crossed thigh bones

explanation.surface: A badge with a crosswise design, linked to another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: The pirate flag at 1 across bears a skull over two thigh bones laid across each other, so the emblem lies transverse.
explanation.definitionFit: The two crossed bones under the skull on a pirate flag lie crosswise.
